title: Vital Signs for Psychosis: Personalized Longitudinal Markers of Psychosis Severity Using Automated Speech and Language Analysis
text:
This study aims to develop personalized adaptive models using automated speech/language analysis to
generate precise, objective markers of concurrent psychosis severity. Innovative computational approaches will
extract speech and language representations and use deep learning as well as algorithmic approaches to
optimize individual-level symptom prediction accuracy over time.

title: Neural mechanisms of socially transmitted aggression
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health and the current objective of the NIMH to elucidate the
brain mechanisms underlying affective and social processes such as aggression. The project is conceptually
and technically innovative because it uses cutting-edge techniques to assess the neural pathways and
mechanisms involved in socially transmitted aggression. This project addresses the priority of NIMH to conduct
research on aggression and violence against others that will eventually lead to new diagnostic and
therapeutic strategies to manage pathological anger and violence.

title: Neuro-immune modulation of pain in health and disease
text:
Nociceptors are specialized sensory neurons which detect noxious stimuli. These neurons serve a vital
protective role in organisms at homeostasis, but pathologies leading to hyperactivation of nociceptors leads to
debilitating pain. This project will explore how the innate immune sensor STING regulates pain in steady-state
conditions and in head and neck cancer. This project will substantiate STING pathway agonists as a
therapeutic strategy for cancer pain through bidirectional neuro-immune signaling. Completion of this project
will accelerate the translation of STING agonists as cancer pain therapy.

title: Development of a Trans-tympanic Endolysin for Noninvasive Treatment of Otitis Media
text:
Otitis media is one of the most common childhood infections and a leading global driver of antibiotic use. This
project will develop a noninvasive biologic that uses a naturally derived antimicrobial enzyme fused to a transport
peptide to cross the intact eardrum and kill the Streptococcus pneumoniae that cause middle-ear
infections. Results could reduce antibiotic use and introduce a new strategy for treating infections behind intact
biological barriers.

title: WP2 - Define and Synthesize
text: RESEARCH ABSTRACT Cancer Grand Challenges Connecting DNA Adducts, Unexplained Mutational Signatures, and Cancer Etiologies (CAUSE) Host Institution: University of California, San Diego Background: Genome sequencing of thousands of cancers has identified over 100 distinct mutational signatures—recurring patterns of somatic mutations that reflect mutagenic processes. While some have known causes, most—including key cancer-driving signatures—remain unexplained. These include endogenous ubiquitous age-associated signatures (e.g., SBS5), tissue-specific processes (e.g., SBS40), and geography-associated patterns likely linked to unknown environmental exposures (e.g., SBS12, SBS89). Biochemically, most somatic mutations arise from misrepair or replication across damaged DNA (i.e., DNA adducts). Cells experience tens of thousands of DNA adducts daily—from both endogenous metabolism and environmental exposures. While most are accurately repaired, some persist leading to permanent changes in the DNA sequence (i.e., somatic mutations). As a result, cancer genomes preserve a durable, but mechanistically obscured, record of genotoxic damage. Understanding the origins of unexplained mutational signatures requires identifying the initiating DNA adducts and dissecting how their formation, persistence, and processing shape mutational patterns. Aims: The Connecting Adducts, Unexplained Signatures, and Cancer Etiologies (CAUSE) project aims to mechanistically understand unexplained mutational signatures by systematically identifying specific DNA adducts and linking them to the mutations they generate. CAUSE will build a high-throughput discovery platform that integrates chemistry, biology, genomics and cutting-edge technologies. The project will focus on three mutagenic contexts: (1) endogenous processes underlying signatures like SBS5 and SBS40, (2) likely environmental exposures driving tissue- and geography-specific patterns like SBS12 and SBS89, and (3) chemotherapy-induced DNA adducts, which will be used as a controlled benchmark. The proposed approaches are broadly applicable and will help uncover the origins of many unexplained mutational signatures while advancing next-generation mutagenesis technologies such as a reimagined Ames test. Methods: CAUSE will integrate human tissue analysis with diverse experimental systems—including in vitro assays, cell lines, and mouse models—across seven coordinated modules: (1) mass spectrometry to detect diverse DNA adducts; (2) structural characterization via chemical synthesis and microcrystal electron diffraction; (3) genome-wide lesion mapping using Endo-seq, long-read sequencing, and polymerase-stalling enrichment; (4) single-molecule reporter assays of misrepair in defined repair contexts; (5) biochemical perturbations in Xenopus cell-free systems to dissect repair mechanisms; (6) genetic perturbations in animal models to dissect damage and repair pathways; and (7) interpretable AI to model how lesion features and repair status predict mutational outcomes. Impact: CAUSE will generate the first mechanistic atlas linking DNA adducts to mutational signatures. This foundational resource will enable causal attribution, clarify age- and exposure-related mutagenesis, and shift mutational signature research from observational to actionable—transforming cancer prevention, diagnosis, and care.

title: A multimodal approach for precision immuno-oncology in lymphoma treated with CAR-T cells
text:
Cellular therapies, such as CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor T-cells (CAR-T), are at the forefront of
large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) treatment, but the majority of treated patients will ultimately experience disease
recurrence or progression. This multidisciplinary study aims to better understand why CAR-T therapy
sometimes fails, despite very promising results in some patients. We seek to understand how tumor genomic
composition drives resistance to CAR-T and will synthesize clinical, molecular, and imaging data using
computational tools to predict the likelihood of response to CAR-T and to identify biomarkers to personalize
patient care.

title: Selective treatment of acute myeloid leukemia with radioimmunotherapies targeting the active conformation of integrin beta-2
text:
Acute myeloid is a commonly-diagnosed blood cancer with an unfortunately poor prognosis for many patients.
Our team has recently discovered a new therapeutic target for this disease and developed a new type of anti-
cancer drug, called a radioimmunotherapy, that can attack this target and eliminate leukemia cells in a
powerful but selective fashion. Here we aim to further test the anti-cancer effects, as well as possible toxicities,
of this approach, with the goal of conducting a future clinical trial to benefit patients in need if results here are
successful.

title: SIRT5 inhibitors and degraders as novel treatments for Ewing sarcoma
text:
The proposed studies are relevant to public health, because discovery of novel means to treat Ewing sarcoma,
exerting fewer deleterious sequelae in survivors, represents a significant unmet need in pediatric oncology. This
work is thus relevant to NIH’s mission, in the context of supporting research to identify cures for human disease.

title: Support for CryoEM and CryoET Development in the Ludtke Lab
text:
This grant works to improve methods for cryo electron microscopy and tomography, to image cells and
molecules at subnanometer resolution, 100-1000x finer than the best optical microscopes. This method can
directly visualize processes like viral infection or cancer at a cellular level with sufficient resolution to see
molecular interactions. The methods developed here will help extend these methods to extract information
about not only static structure, but motion and interactions between molecules at the same high resolutions.

title: Synaptic Mechanisms underlying sex-differences in alcohol use disorder
text:
Despite the relevance of the pro-stress corticotropin-releasing factor and norepinephrine and
the anti-stress nociceptin systems in the sexually dimorphic behavioral aspects of AUD, their
sex-specific cellular mechanisms and interactions in the amygdala have not been fully
delineated. Thus, this proposal will elucidate the neuroadaptive changes induced by ethanol
dependence and withdrawal in these systems in the amygdala. Identifying the potential
neuroadaptations occurring with chronic alcohol is essential for the development of more
effective targeted pharmacotherapeutics for treatment of AUD sufferers.

title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Mechanisms and Therapeutics
text:
Neurodevelopmental disorders affect one in six children in industrialized countries, yet effective treatments are
limited and the underlying mechanisms driving these conditions are still not well defined. This Keystone
Symposia conference on Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Mechanisms and Therapeutics will span basic
mechanisms to translational pipelines, examining biological and environmental contributors, exploring potential
therapies and highlighting innovative technologies that will advance these frontiers. By bringing together basic,
translational and clinical researchers with patient advocates, the meeting will foster cross-disciplinary
collaborations across genetics, functional genomics, circuit neuroscience and therapeutic development, while
training the next generation of researchers and advancing insights toward future clinical applications.

title: Identification of isoform-specific WT1 interaction partners
text:
Wilms’ tumor 1, or WT1, is an important regulator of kidney development and is critical for maintenance of the
adult podocyte. Human mutations in WT1 lead to a spectrum of clinical phenotypes including heavy proteinuria,
progressive kidney dysfunction, risk of Wilms tumor and gonadoblastoma, and disorders of sexual differentiation.
Although the downstream transcriptional targets of WT1 have been the subject of prior studies, our
understanding of the factors that modulate WT1 function is poor. In addition, there are at least 36 WT1 isoforms
arising from alternative splice sites, and the distinct cellular roles of these isoforms are not well understood. The
aim of this proposal is to apply proteomic and cell biology techniques to identify WT1-interaction proteins, study
how these interactions are disrupted with WT1 patient variants, and to elucidate the differential functions of two
main WT1 isoforms. These studies will provide a better understanding of WT1 biology and could lead to the
development of novel therapeutic strategies for patients with WT1-related kidney disease.

title: Single-molecule nanopore-based identification of methylome signatures in cfDNA for early colorectal cancer detection
text:
Early detection of cancer is challenging due to poor adherence to screening schedules and poor sensitivity of
existing methods. Using novel techniques for non-invasive detection of cancer, we will sequence epigenetic
signatures found in the cell-free DNA found in the plasma fraction of blood. Using a combination of cell-free DNA
from patients with a cancer diagnosis and pre-diagnostic plasma from the PLCO Screening Trial, we will
determine the overall benefit of our new technology.

title: Clock Control of Muscle Glucose Metabolism and HIF Activity
text:
The widespread incidence of metabolic disease, including obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus, has become a
major global public health challenge. Evidence suggests that disrupted sleep and feeding cycles, common in
shift and night workers, increase susceptibility to these disorders. In turn, metabolic diseases and aging can also
disrupt circadian rhythms. The goal of this proposal is to advance our understanding of the bidirectional link
between circadian rhythms and nutrient stress in obesity, a condition marked by muscle wasting, glucose
intolerance, and weakness, especially in older individuals. We propose to test whether muscle circadian
disruption obesity and aging impairs adaptation to nutrient stress through regulation of the hypoxia inducible
factor pathway, accelerating the loss of muscle mass, regenerative capacity, and function.

title: Inhalation Delivery of Exosome and microRNA Therapy for Lung Fibrosis
text:
Pulmonary fibrosis is characterized by formation of fibrotic lesions in the lung, eventually resulting in scarring
and progressive loss of lung function, and despite some newer treatments patients still have a median survival
rate of only 3-5 years once diagnosed. Inhalation of exosomes derived from stem cells offers a promising
therapeutic strategy by promoting endogenous repair and mitigating pulmonary fibrosis. Here in this proposed
study, we plan to establish the therapeutic role of lung stem cell-derived exosomes in treating pulmonary
fibrosis and determine the active principal microRNA contents in the exosomes that responsible for the
regenerative activities.

title: Cell Biology Core
text: The Cell Biology/Morphology Core provides BADERC investigators with technical support, equipment, advice and expertise for cell biological, immunocytochemical and morphological studies related to cell/membrane biology and signal transduction; cellular immunology and islet cell biology; and vascular and endothelial cell biology. The Core is located within the MGH Program in Membrane Biology facility on the 8th floor of the Simches Research Center, which is adjacent to the MGH main campus. The Core Director, Dr. Brown, is an expert in the area of membrane biology, membrane proteins, and intracellular trafficking. He has a long and well-documented track record of operating Core facilities at MGH over the past 25 years, including this BADERC Core for over 20 years. The goal of this Core is to provide access to integrated cellular imaging solutions and related expertize for problems in Diabetes and other BADERC-targeted research areas that few or no isolated laboratories have the resources to develop individually. The Cell Biology Core is designed, therefore, to maximize the use and availability of specialized pieces of equipment, that are not only prohibitively expensive for many laboratories, but that also require expensive and regular maintenance, and appropriate technical expertise to use. The Core performs all aspects of microscopy from routine immunofluorescence imaging, confocal microscopy, and (immuno)electron microscopy. The Core is especially proud of its record in successfully attracting NIH Shared Instrumentation Grants (SIGs) and institutional support over the years. With support of Core users, we have obtained 6 SIGs in little more than 12 years, the most recent of which was a $450K award in 2016 for a new Zeiss LSM800 Airyscan confocal platform that offers high sensitivity/high resolution imaging and analysis capabilities to BADERC users. Our other major confocal platform, a Nikon A1R confocal system, offers real time imaging in a temperature controlled chamber, fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and a SIG (for $300K) that was submitted in May 2021 to request major upgrades received an outstanding score of 20 and should be funded. We also offer laser cut microdissection and total internal reflection imaging. We also offer routine embedding and sectioning, and basic immunofluorescence incubation expertize. A major and important objective of the Core is to provide training of key personnel from participating laboratories, a strategy that has worked very successfully over the prior funding periods. Dr. Brown and his highly-qualified technical support staff have well-established and proven procedures for maximizing Core use in the context of varied projects and specific experimental requirements. We pay special attention to quality control procedures for image capture and analysis, and we have protocols for antibody verification to comply with current Rigor and Reproducibility standards. The bottom line is that this Core continues to work smoothly, as in the past. Its use has resulted in several hundred publications over that time that contain images taken by Core staff, or by trained users, including over 90 in the previous BADERC funding period. We expect this to continue and increase based on the usage proposed in this application.

title: Therapeutic Targeting of WDR5 in the Glioblastoma Perivascular Niche
text:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant primary brain tumor and among
the most lethal due to their recurrence and therapeutic resistance. These properties are associated with a GBM
stem cell (GSC) fraction present within distinct microenvironmental niches of the tumor and we have identified
the protein WDR5 as specifically essential for GSCs to grow and maintain stem-cell-like biology in GSC-rich
niches of GBM tumors. The successful completion of this proposal will yield an understanding of the roles of
WDR5 in GBM niche biology and an appraisal of the therapeutic efficacy of inhibiting WDR5 in GBM.

title: Comprehensive characterization of immune signaling networks in single-cells by joint quantification of proteins, protein complexes and mRNA
text:
This proposal describes the improvement and adaptation of a high throughput single cell analysis
technology for simultaneous and multiplexed measurement of proteins, protein complexes and mRNA in
thousands of individual cells, and studying key hypotheses on the development and signaling in hematopoietic
stem cells and germinal center B cells. We will characterize thousands of key protein species regulating pro-
inflammatory signaling responses and development in cells from the hematopoietic lineage and the germinal
center, and combine this data with mathematical modeling and live-cell imaging to understand mechanisms
underlying signal-specific gene regulation, variability and dynamics. Our practical and broadly applicable
technology will rapidly and quantitatively evaluate a vast space of proteomic states, generate improved insight on
the signaling and evolution of immune networks, and make a substantial impact into understanding and modeling
of infection, autoimmunity, immune development and emergence of drug resistance.

title: Development of AI-Assisted digital twin system for phonosurgery
text:
Phonosurgery is designed to improve and restore the voice, often through mechanical correction of laryngeal
configuration. Although the procedures usually result in vocal improvement, optimal treatment still remains a
challenge. In this project, we propose to develop an innovative AI-enabled digital twin algorithm, which will
realize a first-of-its-kind computer model that can represent participant-specific physiology and anatomy and
provide high-precision prediction for simulation-assisted phonosurgery.

title: Revealing environmental chemical exposome in a diverse prenatal population and relationships to maternal and perinatal health (REVEAL)
text:
relationships to maternal and perinatal health (REVEAL)
Our proposal builds on our original R01 by advancing analytical chemistry and computational techniques to
characterize more fully the prenatal chemical exposome and its links to adverse maternal and perinatal health
outcomes. For our renewal project, we propose to expand our study population by analyzing an additional 750
2nd trimester pregnancy samples, 300 of the samples matched to our original 3rd trimester samples and use an
improved nontargeted analysis workflow to identify and quantify novel exogenous and endogenous chemical
exposures. We will use new computational approaches to quantify concentrations of ~500 chemicals and
evaluate relationships between multiple exogenous chemical exposures, endogenous effect biomarkers, and
maternal and perinatal health outcomes, focusing on gestational diabetes and adverse pregnancy outcomes,
providing unprecedented data to inform public health interventions to prevent harmful chemical exposures.
